articles.title: After losing his wife in 2014, a Wisconsin farmer planted 4.5 miles of sunflowers; their seeds later helped raise money for cancer research
articles.summary: US News: After losing his wife to cancer, Don Jaquish turned a shared dream into reality by planting 4.5 miles of sunflowers along Highway 85, creating a stunning memorial that raises funds for cancer research.
articles.body: After losing his wife, Babbette, in 2014, Wisconsin farmer Don Jaquish turned a dream they had shared into one of the region's most memorable living memorials. Babbette had loved sunflowers and had imagined planting them along Wisconsin Highway 85 so that motorists could enjoy the bright yellow flowers. At the same time, the harvested seeds could eventually help people affected by cancer. Her idea became especially meaningful after she was diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2006. Over the following years, she underwent treatments and clinical trials while continuing to support the idea of using sunflowers to raise money for cancer-related causes. She died in 2014, leaving Don to decide what could be done with the dream they had discussed together.After Babbette's death, Don decided that planting the sunflowers would be more than a personal tribute. He wanted the project to reflect her love of the flowers as well as her interest in helping other people facing cancer. .In summer 2015, he rented land from neighbouring farms along Highway 85 near Eau Claire, Wisconsin, and planted the sunflowers across nearly 400 acres, creating a 4.5-mile stretch of yellow flowers. According to an account of the project published by Wisconsin Life, Don rented land from neighbouring farms and planted the sunflower fields the following summer, turning Babbette's favourite flower into a large public memorial. What had once been a private idea between husband and wife had become a memorial visible to people travelling through the area.A 4.5-mile corridor of sunflowersThe scale of the planting made Babbette's favourite flower highly visible. The sunflowers grew along both sides of Highway 85, creating a long yellow corridor through the Wisconsin countryside. Don had chosen the location because the flowers could be seen by people travelling along the road, allowing the memorial to reach far beyond the family's own farmland. When the plants reached full bloom during the summer, the fields attracted attention from local residents, motorists and visitors who stopped to photograph the unusual landscape. The project also carried a personal meaning that went beyond its size. Don had described sunflowers as a flower that suited Babbette's personality, recalling her warmth and the way she could brighten a room. She had become known in the community as the âSunflower Lady,â and the flowers were already closely associated with the couple's farming life before her death. Her idea, therefore, grew from something personal and familiar rather than from a project Don conceived only after she was gone.Turning Babbette's idea into Seeds of HopeBabbette's original idea also involved using sunflower seeds to help others affected by cancer. She had understood the importance of cancer research and clinical trials through her own treatment, and Don later worked to turn that part of her vision into a charitable project. The family created Babbette's Seeds of Hope, with the intention of selling sunflower seeds and directing part of the proceeds toward hospitals, cancer research and patient advocacy. The project gave the fields a purpose beyond remembrance: the flowers could generate support for people facing the same disease that Babbette had battled for years.The first harvest brought another emotional stage to the project. Once the bright flowers faded and the growing season ended, the sunflowers had to be harvested like an ordinary agricultural crop. Don used farm machinery to collect the seeds, which could then be packaged and sold. During the summer, the fields served as a giant memorial that filled the highway with colour; later, the same plants became a source of funds for the charitable purpose Babbette had imagined. According to Wisconsin Life's account of Babbette's Seeds of Hope, the nonprofit had raised more than $50,000 for cancer research by 2018, showing how the memorial had grown into an ongoing fundraising effort.The fields became a community memorialThe sunflower project expanded beyond Don's original tribute. News and photographs of the enormous planting spread widely, bringing attention to both Babbette's story and the charitable purpose behind the fields. People who had never met her could see the flowers and learn why they had been planted. For the Jaquish family, the response also showed how a deeply personal loss could become something that connected them with other families affected by cancer. The project continued in later years through Babbette's Seeds of Hope. The sunflower fields became associated with seasonal events that allowed visitors to experience the flowers more directly. In 2016, a sunflower maze created as part of the tribute attracted thousands of visitors, with donations supporting cancer research. The family's efforts eventually gave the memorial a recurring role in the community rather than limiting it to a single summer. Each new planting brought back the image that had become associated with Babbette and gave the family another opportunity to connect the flowers with cancer support.The continuing project also allowed other people to attach their own memories to the fields. Visitors came not only because the sunflowers created an unusual sight along the highway but also because the story behind them gave the landscape an emotional meaning. The fields represented a woman who had spent years fighting cancer and wanted to use something she loved to help others. For people who had lost relatives or friends to the disease, the sunflower project offered a visible reminder that grief could be turned into an act of support.A living tribute that carried her idea forwardWhat Don created in 2015 was more than a field of flowers. It combined Babbette's love of sunflowers, her experience with cancer and her wish to contribute to research and patient support. The scale of the planting made the tribute visible from the highway, while the harvest gave the project a practical charitable purpose. The family continued the tradition in later years, keeping the connection between the flowers and Babbette's memory alive.Babbette never saw the 4.5-mile stretch of sunflowers that eventually carried her name, but the project allowed Don and their family to complete an idea she had once imagined. The fields transformed an ordinary stretch of Wisconsin farmland into a seasonal memorial that brought together agriculture, remembrance and charity. Each summer bloom recalled Babbette's favourite flower, while the work surrounding the harvest helped continue the purpose behind her dream. Don's decision to plant nearly 400 acres turned that idea into something visible across miles of Wisconsin farmland.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP on Wednesday attacked leader of opposition in Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, over his recent âsmash the patriarchyâ remark, accusing him of hypocrisy and questioning whether he applies the same principle within his own Congress party.Addressing a press conference, BJP leader and MP Bansuri Swaraj referred to Congress leaderâs August 22 remarks at an event in Pune, where he spoke about challenging patriarchal attitudes and restrictions placed on women.âOn August 22, Leader of Opposition (LoP) Rahul Gandhi tried to create a new false narrative in this country. He says, âSmash the patriarchy.â I am all for it,â Swaraj said.âBut I want to ask Rahul Gandhi ji, do you limit the slogan of âsmash the patriarchyâ only to the stage in Pune? Do you practise political patriarchy within your own Congress party?â she added.Swaraj accused Rae Bareli MP of lacking a âvisionâ and âpositive agendaâ, alleging that he uses material prepared by his research team to mislead voters and young people.BJP cites remarks against Kangana, Hema MaliniSwaraj said the Congress should begin by examining its own record if it wants to challenge patriarchy.She cited the controversy involving Congress leader Supriya Shrinate's social media account after BJP MP Kangana Ranaut was given the party ticket from Mandi during the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. Swaraj described the remarks posted from the account as âextremely objectionableâ.She also referred to comments made by Congress leader Randeep Surjewala about BJP leader and actor Hema Malini at a rally in Kaithal in April 2024.Swaraj said Surjewala was subsequently barred from campaigning for 48 hours following action over the remarks.âBut Rahul Gandhi did not âsmash the patriarchyâ then either. There was no such statement from him. Instead, he once again chose to remain silent,â she said.Swaraj also criticised Rahul over what she described as a âhighly objectionable jokeâ involving Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy, saying Gandhi had participated in it along with Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit.âIt does not befit the leader of opposition of the country to make such statements. It appears that leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi now makes statements solely for their meme and reel value,â Swaraj said.BJP MP further said, "I want to ask Rahul Gandhi, why is there not a single woman leader in Karnataka and Himachal? Why did he oppose the Women's Reservation Bill? And you are talking about women empowerment?"Highlighting Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governance model centered on women-led development, Swaraj stated, "You constantly criticize Narendra Modi, but he is a leader committed to empowering women. Currently, 48 percent of Indiaâs women are leading startups around the world. Rahul Gandhi, I am calling you out for your misogyny. This nation deserves a better Leader of the Opposition than you, Mr. Rahul Gandhi."What Rahul Gandhi said about patriarchyCongress MP's remarks came during the Congress' âChhatron Ki Goonjâ campaign in Pune, where he addressed thousands of women and girl students.He said the campaign was aimed at challenging a patriarchal system that, according to him, gives men greater freedom while imposing restrictions on women.Former Congress president referred to a video of PM Modi that he said was released after a protest at Jantar Mantar. He alleged that the Prime Minister was âculturally shockedâ when girls protesting used cuss words but had no objection to boys using similar language.âOur fight is against such a mindset. We do not want a country which gives all the freedom to men, while women continue to live in a controlled environment. We will work together to end the patriarchal system in India,â Rahul said.In an Instagram story, Congress leader had also defended actor Kriti Sanon amid criticism of her outfit in a Raksha Bandhan advertisement, saying, âWhat a woman wears, what she does and where she goes â is her choice.âHe added, âStop trolling women for exercising their freedom,â using the hashtag âsmash the patriarchyâ.The remarks followed criticism of Sanon's attire in a jewellery advertisement, including from BJP MP Kangana Ranaut.Sanon subsequently questioned why women continued to be told what to wear and said, âCulture & Traditions are in her heart, not in her neckline!âGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Work began in 1928 on New York Cityâs first municipal airport; today, Floyd Bennett Field spans more than 1,300 acres of grassland and marsh
articles.summary: US News: Floyd Bennett Field was intended to give New York City its own municipal airport when construction began in 1928. Today, the former airfield is part o.
articles.body: Floyd Bennett Field was intended to give New York City its own municipal airport when construction began in 1928. Today, the former airfield is part of Gateway National Recreation Area and covers more than 1,300 acres of grassland, saltmarshes, tidal mudflats and former aviation facilities. The site in southeastern Brooklyn has changed dramatically since the first airport work began. Its runways and hangars once handled commercial and record-setting flights, and it later became a major naval aviation site before the National Park Service took over the property. The history of Floyd Bennett Field is therefore a record of how one piece of New York City land moved from marshland and landfill to aviation center, military installation and urban recreation area.Construction began in 1928, but the airport opened laterNew York City began transforming the area around Barren Island in 1928, and the project involved waterways, marshes and newly placed fill, as city officials sought to establish an airport within New York's boundaries. The National Park Service's detailed history says the airport was named for naval aviator Floyd Bennett, who had been part of Commander Richard E. Byrd's 1926 flight over the North Pole. Bennett had received the Congressional Medal of Honor and died in 1928 from pneumonia that developed after injuries from an earlier plane crash.Construction took about three years, and the airport was dedicated on May 23, 1931, rather than opening as a completed municipal airport in 1928. The finished complex included concrete runways, four hangars and an administration building that served as the terminal. The site also included facilities for seaplanes, which reflected the importance of Jamaica Bay to the airport's design. A National Park Service historic district account notes that the airport was constructed between 1928 and 1931 by the city's Department of Docks. The project included two main runways, each 100 feet wide, while additional runways were added later.The airport became a center for record-setting flightsFloyd Bennett Field never became the commercial success city officials had hoped for, and New York eventually developed another municipal airport closer to the city's transportation network. That did not make the Brooklyn airfield irrelevant, since between 1931 and 1939, 26 flights that attempted to circle the world or cross the Atlantic began or ended at Floyd Bennett Field, according to the National Park Service.The field also attracted aviators attempting long-distance records. Its location and facilities gave pilots a major base for flights during the period when aviation records were drawing widespread public attention. The airport's role changed as New York expanded its aviation infrastructure. Municipal Airport No. 2, now LaGuardia Airport, opened in 1939. Floyd Bennett Field was subsequently sold to the U.S. Navy, and that transition marked the end of its first chapter as New York City's municipal airport.The Navy took over, and the airfield became a military siteOn June 2, 1941, Naval Air Station New York was dedicated at Floyd Bennett Field, and the Navy expanded the site and continued using it through and after World War II. After the war, the facility became a Naval Air Reserve Training Station in 1946. It was later redesignated as a Naval Air Station within the Naval Air Reserve System, with Navy and Marine squadrons based there and reserve personnel training at the field.The Navy finally deactivated Floyd Bennett Field in 1971. The following year, the property became part of Gateway National Recreation Area under the National Park Service. That transfer changed the purpose of the land again, since instead of serving primarily as an airport or military installation, the site became part of a large urban national recreation area surrounding Jamaica Bay.The former airfield now includes grassland and saltmarshThe National Park Service now describes the area as containing more than 1,300 acres of grassland, saltmarshes, tidal mudflats, a marina and the former airfield. The original control tower and terminal building survive, with the terminal now operating as the William Fitts Ryan Visitor Center. The National Park Service manages the grasslands as habitat, and the site's open landscape supports birds and other wildlife in an area surrounded by one of the country's largest metropolitan regions.Some of the historic aviation structures also remain. The National Park Service is rehabilitating Hangars 3 and 4 as part of a $25 million project intended to preserve the buildings and their Art Deco-era commercial aviation architecture. Visitors can now use parts of the former airport for activities including biking, fishing, bird watching, archery and other recreation. The field is open daily, according to the National Park Service.Floyd Bennett Field is therefore still recognizable as an aviation site, but its function has changed almost completely. The runways and surviving buildings preserve the airport's past, while the surrounding grasslands, saltmarshes and tidal areas have become part of New York City's urban park landscape. The airport once gave New York its first municipal aviation facility and is now one component of a national recreation area, with more than 1,300 acres serving purposes far removed from the city's original plans for the site.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Raids & kidnapping drills: How Chinese students are preparing for college in Trump's USA
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For most Chinese teenagers preparing to leave for American universities, the final months before departure are all about packing clothes, buying the r.
articles.body: For most Chinese teenagers preparing to leave for American universities, the final months before departure are all about packing clothes, buying the right laptop and saying goodbye to family.But some are being taught what to do if armed men burst into their rooms.According to a report by South China Morning Post, private summer camps in China are simulating encounters with US immigration authorities, including fake Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids.The message to students is stark: once they arrive in America, they must be prepared not only for academic pressure and culture shock, but also for an immigration system that has become unpredictable and hostile.The unusual training reflects a much broader shift in the way some Chinese families are thinking about American higher education.For decades, admission to a US university represented the culmination of an intensely competitive academic journey. Now, amid President Donald Trump's sweeping immigration crackdown, some parents are treating the journey as a potential security risk as well.Surviving in the USAReport of such summer camps have emerged against a backdrop of rapidly changing US immigration rules and a heightened political focus on foreign students.The Trump administration has tightened scrutiny of international students, expanded visa vetting and taken steps to make it easier for immigration authorities to act against people whose status is questioned.In 2025, the administration moved to terminate thousands of student records in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), triggering lawsuits and widespread anxiety on US campuses. The government subsequently restored access for many students whose records had been terminated, while maintaining that it had not reversed individual visa revocations.The administration also announced a tougher approach to Chinese student visas, saying it would aggressively revoke visas for some Chinese students and increase scrutiny of future applications from China and Hong Kong. Student and exchange-visitor applicants were also subjected to expanded vetting, including scrutiny of their social media presence.This has created a new calculation for Chinese families sending their children to the US.A student who has spent years preparing for university can now find that admission is only one hurdle.Getting a visa, passing security checks, maintaining legal status and avoiding behaviour that could attract immigration scrutiny have become equally important concerns.The psychological effect is significant.Students are being encouraged to understand their rights, carry documentation, think carefully about their digital footprint and know what to do if approached by immigration officers.For some families, however, the precautions have gone much further.Why Chinese parents are especially anxiousChinese students occupy a unique position in the American higher-education system.According to data cited in recent reporting, 265,919 Chinese students were enrolled at US institutions during the 2024-25 academic year. Together, Chinese and Indian students accounted for 53% of all international students in US higher education.But Chinese students also sit at the intersection of two increasingly sensitive issues: immigration and US-China national security competition.Washington has repeatedly raised concerns about technology transfer, espionage, intellectual property and China's military-civil fusion strategy. Beijing, meanwhile, has accused Washington of discriminating against Chinese students and restricting normal academic exchanges.For an ordinary teenager heading to college, the geopolitical confrontation can feel distant. But the consequences can become personal when visa decisions, social media checks or immigration enforcement enter the picture.In 2025, the number of F-1 student visas issued to Chinese applicants fell sharply. One analysis cited by US media estimated that visas issued to Chinese applicants between May and August 2025 were 46% lower than during the comparable period in 2017.That decline has reinforced fears that studying in America is becoming less predictable.China's government has itself objected to the new restrictions. After the US announced its latest student-visa changes in July 2026, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian called them discriminatory and said Beijing reserved the right to take reciprocal measures.For families who have already paid large sums for American education, the question is no longer simply whether their child can get into a US university.It is whether the child can safely and legally remain there long enough to graduate.The four-year clockThe latest change could make that anxiety even more acute.In July, the Department of Homeland Security announced a final rule ending the decades-old "duration of status" system for international students.Previously, students on F-1 visas could generally remain in the United States for the duration of their academic programme as long as they maintained their status.Under the new system, international students will generally receive a fixed period of admission of no more than four years, subject to extensions. The rule is scheduled to take effect in September.The administration says the change is designed to combat visa abuse and strengthen national-security oversight. DHS has argued that the old system allowed foreign students to remain in the country without sufficiently regular government review.Universities and immigration advocates see it differently.They point out that many doctoral, medical and research programmes routinely last longer than four years. Students could therefore face additional applications and uncertainty in the middle of their academic careers. The new rules also restrict some changes of academic programme or institution.For Chinese parents, the implication is straightforward: getting their child into an American university may no longer mean the child is secure there for the duration of the degree.There is now another deadline to worry about.And then comes the question of stayingFor many international students, the attraction of an American education has never been limited to the classroom.The possibility of gaining professional experience after graduation through Optional Practical Training, or OPT, has been an important part of the calculation.But even that pathway is now facing uncertainty.The Trump administration has considered imposing a $100,000 fee on international students seeking to work in the United States after graduation through OPT, according to a Wall Street Journal report. The proposal remains under discussion and is not established policy, but its emergence has added another layer of uncertainty for prospective students.The cumulative effect is powerful.A Chinese student planning to attend a US university may now have to think about admission, visa approval, social-media screening, immigration status, the four-year limit, possible extensions and the rules governing post-graduation employment.That is a very different proposition from the one presented to previous generations.The fear goes beyond ICEPerhaps the most striking aspect of the reported training camps is that some of the exercises are not even directly about immigration law.The kidnapping drills point to a deeper anxiety: the belief among some parents that their children will be entering an unfamiliar country where they may be vulnerable and far from home.This fear is amplified by China's enormous distance from the US and by the fact that many students leaving for American colleges are teenagers or young adults experiencing independent life abroad for the first time.The drills therefore combine several anxieties into one: immigration enforcement, crime, political instability, unfamiliar laws and the fear that a young student may not know how to respond in a crisis.It is important, however, not to confuse these fears with evidence that Chinese students routinely face kidnapping or that ICE is conducting indiscriminate raids on foreign students.There is no evidence that such dangers are a normal part of student life in the United States.What the drills reveal is something different: how the perception of risk has changed.Parents do not necessarily need to believe that a kidnapping will happen to decide that their child should know what to do if it does.Likewise, a student does not need to expect an ICE encounter to feel anxious about what would happen if immigration officers questioned their status.The social media problemThe atmosphere surrounding visa screening has also changed how international students behave online.In 2025, international students told the Washington Post that they were deleting posts, unfollowing political accounts and scrutinising years of social-media activity because they feared that jokes, memes, political opinions or other online activity could jeopardise their visa applications.The State Department's expanded vetting policy has made digital behaviour an increasingly important part of the immigration process.For Chinese students, that creates a particularly sensitive environment because virtually every aspect of US-China relations can become politically charged.A student can be academically exceptional and have no connection to politics or national security issues, yet still worry that something posted years earlier could be misunderstood.That produces a form of self-censorship that begins before the student ever boards an aircraft.A new generation arrives in America differentlyThe result is a striking transformation in the psychology of studying abroad.Previous generations of Chinese students often arrived in America with one overriding objective: succeed academically.Today's students may arrive with a second mission: avoid becoming entangled in America's increasingly aggressive immigration and national security machinery.That does not mean Chinese students are abandoning the United States.American universities remain enormously attractive because of their academic reputation, research opportunities and global career networks.But the decision is becoming more complicated.For parents paying tens of thousands of dollars in tuition and sending their children thousands of kilometres away, uncertainty carries a price of its own.The kidnapping drills may therefore be less about preparing students for a specific threat than about preparing them for a world in which the rules appear to be changing faster than families can keep up.The irony is hard to miss.America's universities have long marketed themselves as places where young people from around the world can come to learn, experiment and build their futures.Now, some Chinese teenagers are arriving at those same campuses after being taught what to do if someone breaks into their room, takes their phone or threatens to deport them.That is the real significance of the drills.They are not evidence that America has suddenly become a war zone for Chinese students.They are evidence that the psychological border between immigration enforcement and everyday student life has become much thinner.And as Trump's immigration policies continue to tighten the rules around who can enter, how long they can stay and what they can do after graduation, some Chinese families are responding in the most dramatic way possible: by training their children not just to study in America, but to survive the uncertainty of studying there.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: At least eight killed, hundreds missing after Nepal flash flood
articles.summary: Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with people missing in the neighbouring county of Gyirong.
articles.body:
Nepal sent helicopters to the rescue after a huge flash ⁠flood swept away villages, killing at least eight people and damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said.

Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 from countries including the United Kingdom, the United States, India and Malaysia were reported missing as a result of the flash flood on Wednesday.

The waters were too high for helicopters to land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, with a population of about 50,000, officials said.

“There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” district administrator Narendra ‌Pariyar told the Reuters news agency. “But I cannot say for sure now.”

Pariyar urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi River in the area to seek higher ground, pointing to reports that nearby villages and infrastructure project sites were washed away.

Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with people missing in the neighbouring county of Gyirong after a mudslide ⁠hit a land crossing between China and Nepal, the Xinhua official news agency said.

The mudslide hit China’s Gyirong port, cutting off roads, communications and power in the Shigatse region, Xinhua added, without giving details.

President Xi Jinping urged “all-out” efforts to search ⁠for the missing, and ⁠called for strengthening monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.

Prayash Adhikari, a climate justice activist in Nepal, said that the “devastating” flood has wiped out “whole villages”.

“Hundreds of people are missing,” Adhikari told Al Jazeera from Kathamandu, stating that it wiped out buildings, schools, bridges and highways.

Videos shared by Nepal Police and others on social media showed torrents of muddy water crashing through mountain valleys.

Many people were caught off guard when the flash flood hit, as there was no heavy rainfall, said Kosh Raj Koirala Kway-rarla, an editor of Republica Daily, an English newspaper in Nepal’s capital.

“[People] were at home … several houses have been washed away, swept away by the river,” Kway-rarla told Al Jazeera.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah convened an emergency meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority to take stock of the situation.

“Work has started to take necessary steps in coordination with the medical team, scouts, and Red Cross,” Shah said in a social media post.

The Nepal Army said it had deployed helicopters and disaster response personnel to the affected area.

“The work of collecting details of the damage is under way,” it said in a statement.

The Nepal Electricity Authority said about 430 megawatts of production capacity, including from hydropower and solar facilities, have been damaged.

“The disaster has damaged the production, transmission and distribution facilities of the Authority … resulting in disruption of electricity supply,” it said.

Several highways were also closed, authorities said.

‘Glacial lake outburst’ could be underlying cause

Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused the flash flood.

The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, witnessed maximum flooding on Wednesday, they said.

“The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.

Adhikari told Al Jazeera that early warning systems are crucial to protect communities, said Adhikari.

“This can’t be completely turned around because we are on the verge of climate catastrophe, but still we can protect our communities,” he said.

The ⁠Bhote Koshi River originates in Tibet ⁠and empties into Nepal’s Trishuli River that eventually flows into India as the Gandak River.

A flood last year in the Bhote Koshi River killed nine people, ‌with 24 missing, and washed away the “Friendship Bridge” linking Nepal and China, disrupting transport and trade for several months. That flood ‌was ‌triggered by the draining of a supraglacial lake in Tibet, a regional climate monitor said.

Monsoon rains from June to September regularly trigger deadly floods and landslides across South Asia.

Scientists say climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in the region.

articles.title: Sheffield delivery robots removed from streets as pilot ends
articles.summary: Operator Starship Technologies says the end of the trial is not due to vandalism of the machines.
articles.body:
Self-driving food delivery robots have been taken off the streets after the operator called time on a pilot scheme after just five months.

The six-wheeled machines were launched in parts of Sheffield by Starship Technologies in March in partnership with Uber Eats.

During the short trial the foot-high vehicles kept getting their visibility flags snapped off and some were sprayed with graffiti, as well as attracting complaints that they "got in the way" of pedestrians.

Starship Technologies said it had "paused" the service as its pilot scheme had come to a "natural" end, but insisted the vandalism did not affect the decision to stop.

Delivery robots tasked with carrying supermarket and takeaway orders have become a familiar sight in major UK cities, including Leeds and London.

They have divided opinion, with some people praising their nimbleness and convenience, while critics have complained they obstruct pavements and carry a "sinister" number of cameras.

But while they have become a permanent feature in parts of Leeds, Starship said the service had been halted in Sheffield for now.

As well as the robots themselves falling victim to vandalism in March, a charging station was defaced and traffic cones were placed behind the robots to prevent them from moving .

Ryan Case, public affairs and communication manager at Starship said: "Our pilot in Sheffield has come to an end, and we have paused the service while we review what we've learned.

"There have been a small number of incidents of vandalism, which is disappointing, not least because it affects the local businesses that rely on the robots for deliveries.

"But vandalism wasn't a factor in our decision to pause the service: this was a commercial decision and a natural conclusion to the pilot phase."

articles.title: The Memo: Canada’s Carney gets under Trump’s skin amid trade dispute
articles.summary: The personal is political, it’s said — and it certainly seems to have become so between President Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. articles.body:
The personal is political, it’s said — and it certainly seems to have become so between President Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The two men are at odds as a trade war between the two nations ramps up. On Tuesday, Canada announced the imminent imposition of tariffs on around 700 U.S. products. The new levies, retaliation for fresh U.S. tariffs, are scheduled to kick in Sept. 8.

But there seems to be an element to the struggle between the two leaders that goes beyond the hard numbers and technical minutiae of trade and import duties.

Trump has at times referred to the Canadian prime minister as “Governor Carney” on social media. It’s a none-too-subtle allusion to Trump’s professed desire to make Canada the 51st state of the U.S. But it’s also plainly intended to belittle the Canadian prime minister in a more personal sense.

On Monday, in reference to Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Trump took to social media to write :

“Without the United States, Canada couldn’t survive — It’s where they get all of their money and, because of their current bad leadership, primarily Governor Carney, and his Flunky, Ford, they will not be allowed to keep taking advantage of the United States — Their key to survival.”

In fact, it appears to be, at least in part, Carney’s willingness to stand up to Washington that enrages Trump.

It was the Canadian leader whose team walked away from trade talks between the two nations late last week. In doing so, he confounded predictions from Trump, just days previously, that an agreement would indeed be arrived at between the two sides.

Carney’s move could have been purloined from Trump’s “The Art of the Deal” — at least in its capacity to leave his counterparts wrong-footed. But Carney’s tone of defiance, applauded by many of his own voters, seems sure to aggravate Trump even further.

At a news conference Saturday, Carney contended that the U.S. wanted to add late terms into the deal, which he said were not merely “uneconomic [and] unfair” but “called into question the reliability of any deal.”

Carney, who has also implied that there was a lack of cohesion among the U.S. negotiating team, asserted that, “They asked too much, and they offered too little.”

The suggestion that the U.S. was both disunited and unreliable is exactly the kind of gambit likely to raise Trump’s ire.

Trump’s pique about Carney’s attitude — and his attempts to regain the upper hand — have included more than mere claims that Canada will suffer the most from any trade war.

It has also included an assertion from Trump on social media Tuesday that “Canada has been ‘Ripping Off’ the U.S.A. for decades” and that “I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable.”

The message was Trump’s third referencing Canada before 10 a.m. EDT Tuesday. The previous two had, respectively, accused Carney of being “weak and ineffective” for suggesting Trump was dismissive of French Canadians and suggested that the U.S. was “giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

Adding to the trollish tone of the Lake Ontario suggestion, Trump later shared a map of the body of water in question, with its actual name x-ed out and “Lake America” written in its place.

What Carney makes of such tactics is not that hard to guess.

The urbane Canadian prime minister is about as far removed from Trump in terms of tone or demeanor as it is possible to be.

A graduate of Harvard and Oxford, he first came to major public prominence as the governor of the Bank of Canada almost 20 years ago. He followed up his stint at the helm of his central bank with seven years in the equivalent post on the other side of the Atlantic, as governor of the Bank of England.

Carney’s self-assurance — and his ease among power elites — also showed itself at Davos, Switzerland, in January. The Canadian prime minister’s speech at the World Economic Forum caused a massive stir, despite not mentioning Trump by name.

The headline-grabbing phrase was Carney’s contention that the West, at least, was “in the midst of a rupture, not a transition.” Much of the speech seemed premised on the idea that the United States was no longer the reliable ally it had once been. This, in turn, led Carney to implore the world’s “middle powers” to “act together because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.”

The address — and the praise it received — set off a spat between the two leaders.

Trump, in his own remarks to Davos, struck a peeved tone. He asserted that, “Canada gets a lot of freebies from us.” And he added, in a jab directly at Carney: “Canada lives because of the United States. Remember that, Mark, the next time you make your statements.”

Carney, back in Canada, shot back: “Canada doesn’t live because of the United States. Canada thrives because we are Canadian.”

From that point on, it seems, the stage was set for the drama that is currently playing out.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Missouri grandma ordered to stop serving free breakfasts refuses to back down, 'They are my family'
articles.summary: Kathy Kite says she won't stop serving free breakfast in Harrisburg, Missouri, despite a health department letter saying she needs a permit
articles.body: A Missouri grandmother says she was frightened she could end up in legal trouble after county health officials told her to stop serving free homemade breakfasts without a permit, but she told Fox News Digital she has no intention of giving up the morning tradition that brings her tiny community together. "I'm not gonna stop providing for my community," Kathy Kite of Harrisburg, Missouri, told Fox News Digital in an interview Tuesday. "I wouldn't stop feeding my children, I wouldn't stop feeding my family. I'm not gonna stop feeding my community cause they are my family….This is bigger than that. It's about love and appreciation because they appreciate what I do." Kite has been cooking a free breakfasts for her neighbors and friends since May. In July, she received a letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department that said she needed to obtain a food permit or face possible legal action. YOU SHOULDN’T NEED A PERMIT TO PRAY IN YOUR OWN HOME — THE SUPREME COURT SHOULD AGREE "I got the letter in July, it upset me, because I didn't understand what I was doing wrong," Kite said. "It hurt my feelings, and it upset me because I knew at that point I was afraid I was gonna go to jail because the letter stated that if I didn't stop making breakfast for my community, that I was facing fines and jail, and so I posted it on Facebook and people responded."  The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department denied that their letter threatened jail time, in comments to Fox News Digital. Kite said that after the local gas station where she works stopped serving breakfast following COVID, regular customers kept asking for it, so she invited them to her home and began cooking breakfast for them, herself. Kite said that what began as an early-morning breakfast for a few regulars quickly spread across the town of fewer than 300 people. More residents began stopping by for coffee and breakfast, staying to talk about farming, the weather and childhood memories. The growing sense of community motivated her to wake up even earlier to cook, and soon local mothers were bringing their children by for breakfast before school. ORTHODOX JEW ASKS SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CASE AFTER CITY ALLEGEDLY TARGETED HIS HOME PRAYER GROUP Kite said the letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department says that she must install a commercial kitchen in her home. "In order for me to comply with what they're asking, I would have to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to have a commercial kitchen in my home," Kite said. "I live in a 115-year-old home. It's a beautiful home. I'm not gonna jeopardize the integrity of my home to put a commercial kitchen in to make some free burritos." She said she would welcome city officials into her home so they could see firsthand what she is doing. "Come have a burrito. I'm [not] doing anything wrong. I don't, I just, I can't understand. Come to my home, see my home, and see that my home is not dirty," Kite said. "I don't have cats. I'm not making people sick. I am just a grandma cooking a meal for my friends and family and enjoying life." The Goldwater Institute sent a letter Thursday to the Boone County health department demanding they answer questions by Friday about their legal reasoning. The group said that no lawsuit has been filed to date, but it is on the table. GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS In a statement to Fox News Digital, Dave Roland, Goldwater Institute's director of allied litigation, said, "Kathy’s story is a textbook example of bureaucracy run amok. Citizens should not be required to get the government’s permission before offering passers-by some coffee and a bite to eat while they socialize. The government exists to protect this sort of neighborly kindness, not to punish it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department told Fox News Digital that food permits are not required when providing food for family and friends, but a permit is required when providing food to the public, citing the Missouri food code. "At the time the complaint was received, Ms. Kite’s home had an open sign, tip jar, advertised food on social media and a sign in her yard — all things that are typically associated with a food establishment," the spokesperson said. "No citations or cease-and-desist orders were issued," the statement continued. "We also did not threaten jail time. We sent a letter to Ms. Kite following a complaint we received that food served in her establishment made someone ill. Our role in public health is to work with food establishments to promote safe food practices and prevent food-borne illnesses. There are safe, allowable ways to provide homemade food to the community with and without a food permit. We regularly work together with individuals and businesses who want to provide free food to the community."

articles.title: He Thought $50,000 From Barn Weddings Was Rent. Social Security Saw a Second Job.
articles.summary: A farmer strings lights in his old dairy barn, books $50,000 worth of weddings, and assumes he is collecting rent on property he already owns. Social Securit...
articles.body:
Running barn weddings as a service business rather than as passive rental creates self-employment income that Social Security counts against benefits before full retirement age.

Net profit, not gross revenue, determines Social Security exposure. Deducting expenses from $50,000 in bookings could shrink countable earnings and reduce withheld benefits by thousands.

Benefits withheld before full retirement age aren't permanently lost. Social Security recalculates monthly payments at FRA and eliminates the earnings test entirely afterward.

A 65-year-old farmer restores the old dairy barn on his property, strings lights across the rafters and begins booking weddings from May through October. The land has not paid like it once did, and the barn brings in $50,000 during a good season. He claimed Social Security at 62 and is now 65, and remains two years shy of his full retirement age (FRA), so the earnings test still follows him. He assumes the wedding money is rent from property he already owns. Rent generally stays outside that test.

But he is not simply unlocking the barn and collecting a check. He schedules tours, coordinates vendors, sets up tables, handles parking and cleans up after the last guest leaves. He thought he had rented out a building. In practice, he had given himself a second job.

Rental income from real estate generally stays outside the Social Security earnings test. If the farmer leased the barn to an event company for a fixed amount and stepped away, that income might remain rent. His labor changes the picture.

When a property owner provides substantial services for the customer's convenience, the activity can become a business. The IRS generally directs that income to Schedule C, where revenue is reduced by allowable expenses to determine net profit. That profit is usually subject to self-employment tax. It also becomes the kind of earned income Social Security counts before FRA.

articles.title: Fire kills 14 newborns at major hospital in Pakistan, officials say
articles.summary: Poor enforcement of building safety regulations in Pakistan has been blamed for the high death toll in fires.
articles.body:
A fire at a hospital's maternity ward in a major government hospital in Pakistan's capital killed at least 14 newborn babies early on Wednesday, according to hospital officials and the government.

The fire broke out on the third floor of the Mother and Child Health Ward at the public Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital, according to the district administration.

Rescue officials said the fire broke out at around 6:45 am (3:45 am CEST) after an air-conditioning unit compressor apparently exploded inside the nursery, located in the hospital's gynecology ward.

Sohail Ashraf, the Islamabad chief commissioner, said on X that rescue teams, specialists, police and himself "immediately reached at site and controlled the fire."

At least one baby was reportedly rescued.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and ordered an immediate investigation.

"The loss of children in such circumstances is irreparable," a statement from his office said.

Sharif also expressed his "heartfelt condolences to the families of the innocent children," adding that he was "saddened by this tragic incident.".

Police said the newborns killed in the fire were severely burned, making DNA testing necessary to confirm their identities before their bodies can be released to their families.

The statement came after parents called for the bodies to be handed over immediately.

Fires in large buildings are frequent in Pakistan, often due to poor safety laws and building codes as well as lax enforcement.

articles.title: Les Paulâs 7-acre New Jersey home, studio and workshop sold for $990,000 in July; weeks later the property where he pioneered multitrack recording was demolished, and his son says the family got no warning
articles.summary: US News: The New Jersey home where legendary guitarist and inventor Les Paul lived, worked and helped reshape modern music recording has been demolished, just .
articles.body: The New Jersey home where legendary guitarist and inventor Les Paul lived, worked and helped reshape modern music recording has been demolished, just weeks after the seven-acre Mahwah property was sold for $990,000. The loss drew particular attention because the house was not simply a former celebrity residence; it included the spaces where Paul experimented with sound, developed recording techniques and worked on ideas that would influence generations of musicians and producers. Les Paulâs son, Gene Paul, spoke about the demolition in a Facebook post, saying the family received no advance warning that the property was going to be demolished. He described the loss of the home as deeply painful and questioned how the property had been handled.What was lost with the Mahwah home?The property was sold on July 22, 2026, for $990,000, according to reporting by Stephanie Iken. It was a more than 6,300-square-foot home on seven acres in Mahwah's Deerhaven community. Within weeks, the structure had been demolished. The controversy stems from what the building represented. According to Guitar Player, Les Paul used the Mahwah property as a home, workshop and laboratory, where he developed pioneering multitrack recording techniques, experimented with electric-guitar technology and worked on pickup designs. He and Mary Ford also recorded songs and their television show at the house.For Gene Paul, therefore, the demolition was about more than the disappearance of an old house. In his Facebook post, he described the property as his father's workshop and laboratory and said its destruction was deeply upsetting. He questioned how the property had been handled and why his family had not been given a meaningful opportunity to be involved.His son says the family had no warningIn his Facebook post, Gene Paul said his family was given no advance warning of the demolition and was not given an opportunity to enter the house before it was destroyed. He described seeing his father's former home gutted and questioned why the family had not been consulted about its fate. The loss also raised concerns about what remained inside. A statement from the Les Paul Legacy Group, cited by Guitar Player, said that people close to Paul made a last-minute effort to save historically significant material, including handwritten research notes and Paul's workbenches. According to the group, some of those items were found in rooms that had suffered water damage and mold after years of alleged neglect by the foundation.Those claims have added another layer to the dispute, shifting the conversation beyond the demolition itself to questions about preservation, ownership and responsibility for protecting historically significant spaces.Why the property mattered to music historyLes Paul was far more than a celebrated guitarist. His experiments with sound and recording helped lay the foundations for techniques that later became central to modern music production. At the Mahwah property, his work included pioneering experiments with multitrack recording and electric-guitar technology. The site also became a destination for prominent musicians; famous guitarists visited Paul there to discuss music and technology.That history is why Gene Paul and others have objected to describing the property as simply an old building. Its significance, they argue, lay not only in its association with a famous musician but also in the work that took place within it. The home was also closely connected to Les Paul and Mary Ford's musical and television careers. According to Guitar Player, the couple recorded songs and their television show, Les Paul & Mary Ford at Home, at the Mahwah house.A wider debate over preserving creative historyThe demolition has also sparked a disagreement involving the Les Paul Foundation. According to Guitar Player, the foundation's executive director, Michael Braunstein, defended its preservation efforts, while comments describing the historic property as essentially âfour wallsâ drew criticism from members of the music community, guitar historians and Paul's family. At the centre of the dispute is a larger question: when does a private home become an important part of cultural history?Not every historic site can be preserved indefinitely, and private ownership, maintenance costs and property rights can complicate such decisions. But the Mahwah home had an unusual place in music history because it was also a working laboratory. It was where Les Paul experimented, built, recorded and developed ideas that extended far beyond his own performances. Now the house is gone, leaving behind an increasingly emotional debate about whether more could have been done to protect it, or at least to preserve and recover the objects and spaces that documented Paul's work.For Gene Paul, the issue remains deeply personal. The building was his childhood home and the place where his father worked on some of the innovations that helped shape modern recording and electric-guitar technology. In a Facebook post, he questioned how such an important part of his family's history could disappear without the family receiving advance warning. The demolition has therefore become more than a story about a property sold and later torn down. It is a reminder that places connected to technological and artistic breakthroughs can disappear quickly, leaving historians, fans and family members to consider what should happen when a private property also carries a significant piece of cultural history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Why we should all get used to high household energy bills
articles.summary: The government is under pressure to support billpayers when domestic energy prices predicted to rise further.
articles.body:
Energy bills may have been a long way from our minds through the sweltering summer.

Clothes on a washing line have been drying in minutes. Cold showers have been more tempting than hot ones.

But the latest news and forecasts on gas prices will bring a renewed sense of worry and urgency to families, as well as government ministers.

Energy prices will rise by nearly 4% for millions of households in October. Even more striking is a prediction from the respected consultancy Cornwall Insight of a further 9% increase at the peak of winter in January.

With ongoing volatility in the wholesale gas market sparked by events in the Gulf region, the energy sector says high prices are here to stay.

EDF suggests bills will remain "stubbornly high" at their current level at least until the end of the decade.

High bills have, and continue to, bite. Energy prices have been central to the cost-of-living squeeze.

The typical household's dual-fuel bill is now 70% higher than it was at the start of 2021, before Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

That amounts to around £600 more each year than pre-crisis levels, according to industry body Energy UK.

Inevitably, more and more people have been unable to pay. Unpaid energy debt of more than three months is now at a record high, according to regulator Ofgem.

Suppliers, who chart debt levels for missed payments of a month or more, estimate total unpaid bills and charges to have reached £6bn. By the end of the year, they expect that to rise to £7bn.

The average household in debt, without a repayment plan, owes more than the typical annual bill.

And even if you are not in debt, you pay. Covering the cost of debt already adds about £60 to the average annual bill. Consultancy Baringa says everyone could, on average, be paying £100 to cover the cost of unpaid debts by the end of the year.

So, pressure on the government to help those most in need will only intensify.

Ofgem has a proposed debt relief scheme on the table, and campaigners keep telling them to get on with it, urging the government as to provide funding for it to be implemented.

Charities and the industry also want ministers to introduce a discounted tariff for those who need it most - based on benefits, health and income data.

Energy UK says a targeted plan would cost £1.9bn. That would be much cheaper than the £40bn commitment to protect everyone's bills after Russia invaded Ukraine.

But, who would pay? It could go on everyone else's bills. Or ministers could opt to raise taxes, borrow the money, or cancel spending elsewhere - all of which are tricky political choices.

Those who can have cut back on their energy use to reduce bills in recent years. Thermostats up and down the country have not been set as high as before. Batch cooking is more common.

So much so that Ofgem's official calculations for typical energy consumption were lowered again in July (to 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year).

Millions have shifted onto fixed tariffs, with 35% of billpayers on such a deal.

So, many can justifiably say they have done their bit. Others who are older or who have health conditions might not have the luxury of lowering their energy use.

So, community warm hubs have become popular. Some became cold hubs during the hot summer so people could make use of the air con.

The heatwave has reduced the amount of energy stored across Europe, which needs to be restocked, piling more pressure on prices.

Add to that the huge cost of upgrading the UK's electricity network and you can see why there are predictions of longstanding high energy bills - irrespective of whether a lasting peace in the Iran war brings down the international price of wholesale gas.

In the long-term, the government and Ofgem wants to shift the country away from our reliance on gas, with its volatile international pricing.

Expect lots of fanfare over the sale, for the first time in the UK, of plug-in solar panels.

In the short-term ministers - and the new prime minister - say they are helping where they can, and promising that there is "more to do".

VAT will be cut on electricity bills in October. It means the price of electricity will fall, but that's been more than outstripped by an 8% rise in the price of gas.

In the last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves cut some so-called policy costs and shifted some onto general taxation instead.

Ministers may be tempted to do more of that, but could face be criticised for simply shifting the burden off bills and onto taxes.

So, the options are limited. The new chancellor, John Healey, has choices to make - with lots of calls for help but with limited room for manoeuvre in the public finances.

All eyes will be on his first Budget, which comes soon after those higher autumn energy bills kick in.

The aircraft, operating under the call sign RCH4555, left Riga at around 8.50am and landed in Moscow shortly after 10am.The flight had arrived in Riga on August 23 from Camp Springs, Maryland, home to Joint Base Andrews, a key US military facility associated with presidential air transport.The reported Ratcliffe visit comes against the backdrop of intensifying US-Russia contacts since Donald Trump returned to the White House and pledged to negotiate an end to the Ukraine war.However, repeated visits to Moscow by Trumpâs peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have so far failed to bridge major differences between Russia and Ukraine, particularly over territory. Their planned first visit to Ukraine this week was also postponed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Over 100 Indians missing after flash floods hit Nepal - what we know so far
articles.summary: South Asia News: Over 100 Indians were reported missing after a massive flash flood swept through Nepalâs Rasuwa district near the Tibet border on Wednesday, killing a.
articles.body: Over 100 Indians were reported missing after a massive flash flood swept through Nepalâs Rasuwa district near the Tibet border on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and causing widespread damage to settlements and infrastructure.The sudden surge in the Bhote Koshi River struck the Rasuwagadhi-Timure area at around 9 am local time, affecting Rasuwa as well as parts of neighbouring Nuwakot and Dhading districts.The flooding washed away vehicles, goods, bridges and other infrastructure, while several hydropower projects were also damaged.105 Indians missingAccording to a preliminary list compiled by the Nepal Tourism Board, 384 travellers, including 291 foreign nationals and 93 Nepali nationals, have been reported missing following the flash flood.Of the foreign nationals, 105 are from India. The list also includes travellers from Australia, the Netherlands, the US, Malaysia, the UK and South Africa, while the nationalities of some others are yet to be confirmed.The Tourism Board said the list is preliminary and is being verified in coordination with travel agencies, guides, local authorities and security agencies. It urged travellers and their families not to draw conclusions until the verification process is complete.Kailash Mansarovar pilgrims among those missingA large number of those out of contact are believed to be pilgrims travelling to Tibet for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra.Bashu Kumar Adhikari, managing director of Kathmandu-based Touch Kailash Travels & Tours, said 390 pilgrims, including 93 Nepalis, were scheduled to cross the border on Wednesday.âExcept for a few, we have not been able to establish contact with the pilgrims as of 3pm,â Adhikari said, according to The Kathmandu Post.Sagar Pandey, president of the Trekking Agenciesâ Association of Nepal, said efforts were underway to contact the pilgrims and assess their condition.Several dead, rescue operations under wayAt least eight people have been confirmed dead, while more than 25 people had been rescued by Wednesday afternoon, according to Nepal Army officials cited by local media.Four bodies were recovered from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot and were found near the Trishuli river, according to police.The Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police have been mobilised for search-and-rescue operations. As many as 14 helicopters have been deployed, while drones and sniffer dogs are also being used to locate missing people.The Nepal Army said six people were rescued from Syafrubesi, two from Mailung and four from Dhunche in Rasuwa. It has also set up a treatment centre at the Military Training Centre No 1 in Trishuli to provide emergency medical care.Four Armed Police Force personnel were initially reported missing from Rasuwa, while another report said nine personnel stationed at Timure, near the Nepal-China border, were unaccounted for.Flood alert issued along Gandak river in BiharThe Indian government has issued an advisory after a sudden rise in the water level of Nepalâs Trishuli river at Furke Khola, around 160 km from the Indian border, was reported amid suspected glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) activity near the Nepal-China border.The advisory said the flood wave is expected to move downstream into the Gandak river, with its intensity likely to reduce as it travels. Authorities in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh along the India-Nepal border have been asked to remain alert and closely monitor the situation.Authorities have also been advised to take necessary precautionary measures along the Gandak river. The gates of the Gandak Barrage should be operated in a manner that allows the anticipated floodwater to pass through safely.Amit Shah speaks to Bihar CMIn view of the potential flood threat in Bihar following heavy rainfall in Nepal, Union home minister Amit Shah spoke to Bihar chief minister Samrat Choudhary over the phone, according to news agency ANI.Shah assured the Bihar government of all possible assistance to deal with the situation. The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is also being mobilised to respond to any emergency.UP CM urges districts to remain vigilantUttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath expressed concern over the flood situation in Nepal and directed local authorities in vulnerable districts to remain alert.In a post on X, Yogi said, "The damage caused by the devastating floods in the Bhote Koshi River in Nepal's Rasuwa region is extremely worrying. Prayers to Lord Pashupatinath for the safety of all.""In view of the rise in water levels of the Gandak and Narayani rivers and the possibility of flooding in Uttar Pradesh's districts of Maharajganj and Kushinagar due to its impact, instructions have been issued to the local administration to remain fully vigilant and ensure necessary preparations," he added.What caused the flash flood?The exact cause of the sudden rise in the Bhote Koshi River remains unclear. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology said the flooding was not caused by rainfall in Rasuwa.Officials are examining whether it could have been triggered by a glacial lake outburst flood, a landslide or another event on the Tibetan side of the border.Dinkar Kayastha, information officer at the department, said, âWe are still studying the matter, so the real cause is not yet known.âHe also warned that the risk from the Tibetan side had not disappeared and said, âwe need to be cautious.âOfficials have received informal information that a landslide may have temporarily blocked a river in Tibet before the swollen water burst through, but this has not yet been confirmed.Widespread damage, villages washed awayRasuwa has emerged as the worst-hit district, with Timure and Syafrubesi among the areas suffering extensive damage. Vehicles and goods stored at the customs premises were swept away and a recently built bridge was destroyed.Several settlements along the river have also been affected, including Syaphrubesi, Betrawati, Mailung, Salletar, Shantibazar, Pairebesi, Khalti Basti, Sole, Trishuli and Battar.A bridge in Gajuri in Dhading district was also washed away.The flash flood has severely affected Nepal's trade route with Tibet, with infrastructure at Rasuwagadhi, an important border crossing with China, damaged in the disaster.Hydropower projects damagedThe flooding has also hit Nepal's hydropower sector. According to the Independent Power Producers' Association Nepal, eight operational hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 354 MW and five projects under construction in Rasuwa and Nuwakot were damaged.Among the affected operational projects are the 111-MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, 78-MW Sanjen Khola Hydropower Project and 60-MW Upper Trishuli 3A project.Authorities issue safety warningNepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has placed several downstream districts, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitawan and Gorkha, on high alert.Authorities have urged people living near the Trishuli and other rivers to stay away from riverbanks and move to safer areas. Tourists in the affected regions have also been advised to remain calm, stay informed and follow official safety instructions.As per local media, those needing emergency assistance can contact 1234, 1144 or the Tourist Police at 9851289445, or inform the nearest police or security post, local administration, travel agency, guide or tour operator.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Britain has been warned to prepare for possible Russian retaliation after Prime Minister Andy Burnhamâs visit to Ukraine and the UKâs decision to share technology that could help Kyiv produce long-range missiles.Security sources cited by the Daily Mail have warned that Russia could mount a âdirect responseâ against Britain, amid concerns in Whitehall that Moscow may have underestimated Burnhamâs commitment to Ukraine.A senior source told the newspaper: âThe question being asked is, "How long do we keep poking the bear before it bites?"âThe warning comes after Britain agreed to hand Ukraine blueprints for British-made components used in the Storm Shadow cruise missile, allowing Kyiv to produce the long-range weapon domestically.Russia has reacted angrily to the move, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying on Monday that Britainâs involvement prevented âeven the slightest progressâ towards peace.Peskov also said the Russian military was gathering information on missile production sites in an apparent warning that such facilities could become targets.âBritain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire,â he said.Burnham hit back during his visit to Ukraine, asking: âWho started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?âHis trip to Kyiv was his first official international visit as prime minister, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and chaired a meeting of the âcoalition of the willingâ, established by Britain and France to support Ukraine.The warnings of possible Russian action were reinforced by comments from former Russian deputy foreign minister Andrei Fedorov, who suggested Moscow could consider a âsemi-militaryâ response.Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Fedorov said there was pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin âto undertake Ukraine.ââThey could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources.âThe comments come as Russia itself faces growing pressure from Ukrainian drone strikes, particularly against oil refineries and other critical infrastructure.President Vladimir Putin has issued a decree allowing the Russian state to temporarily take control of critical infrastructure if private owners fail to adequately protect facilities from Ukrainian drone attacks or rebuild damaged sites.The measure covers energy, industrial, communications, transport and logistics facilities, with Kremlin officials on the Afipsky and Novoshakhtinsk oil refineries.Burnham has nevertheless reaffirmed Britainâs support for Kyiv and said he plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to press articles.title: How do navies hunt submarines? NATO's deadly game of detection beneath the waves
articles.summary: International News: NATO navies are once again turning their attention to one of the oldest and most difficult problems at sea, finding and neutralising an adversary's su.
articles.body: NATO navies are once again turning their attention to one of the oldest and most difficult problems at sea, finding and neutralising an adversary's submarines before they can strike. This week, Standing NATO Maritime Group One and Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group One joined Exercise Northern Viking 26 off the coast of Iceland. This was a US-led drill built around defending the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom Gap, one of the most strategically sensitive maritime corridors in the world. The waters between Greenland and Iceland, and between Iceland and Britain, have long served as the primary route through which Russian submarines would have to pass to threaten the North Atlantic. This makes the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap a natural chokepoint for anti-submarine operations since the Cold War.Hunting submarines, however, remains one of the most technically demanding forms of naval warfare. Submarines rely on stealth as their primary defence, and modern anti-submarine warfare has evolved into a layered contest fought largely through sound rather than sight. Passive sonar systems listen for the acoustic signature of a submarine inevitably generates. These acoustic signals are produced by the submarine's engines, propellers and other machinery.On the other hand, active sonar transmits a pulse and interprets its echo to pinpoint a target submarine's range and bearing. Networks of sonobuoys, dropped from patrol aircraft or helicopters, are spaced across a search area to detect and triangulate a submerged contact, while fixed hydrophone arrays on the seabed provide a persistent listening capability across critical corridors.Surface ships, submarines and maritime patrol aircraft all work in tandem, since no single platform can reliably hold a contact on its own, a principle that lies at the very heart of coordinated anti-submarine warfare doctrine. Exercises like Northern Viking underline a wider truth about anti-submarine warfare: detecting and holding a submarine at risk demands persistent coordination between different assets, advanced acoustic technology and an understanding of an operating environment that keeps changing.Since the end of the Second World War, India is the only country which has sunk a submerged submarine in conflict. During the 1971 war, Pakistani submarine PNS Ghazi was sunk by the destroyer INS Rajput outside Visakhapatnam harbour. The Ghazi had been sent to the Bay of Bengal to sink the aircraft carrier INS Vikrant. On the western naval front, Pakistani submarine had torpedoed and sunk the Indian frigate INS Khukri. Since the end of the Second World War many other ships have been sunk by submarines, such as the Argentinian cruiser ARA General Belgrano, which was sunk by a submarine during the Falkland War and the recent sinking of Iranian ship IRIS Dena near the Sri Lankan coast. As both submarines and anti-submarine systems are becoming more advanced, these changes are also making the act of 'killing' a submarine a more difficult task.
